## Why it can throw

`DefaultListableBeanFactory.registerBeanDefinition(String, BeanDefinition)` checks whether a `BeanDefinition` is already registered under the given name (`spring-beans/.../DefaultListableBeanFactory.java:1268-1276`). If one exists and `isBeanDefinitionOverridable(beanName)` returns `false`, it throws `BeanDefinitionOverrideException(beanName, beanDefinition, existingDefinition)` instead of silently replacing it. The same check applies to registering a name that's currently an alias for another bean (lines 1281-1290).

## Configuration that triggers it

`isBeanDefinitionOverridable` (line 1447) simply defers to `isAllowBeanDefinitionOverriding()` (line 279), which returns `!Boolean.FALSE.equals(this.allowBeanDefinitionOverriding)`. So:
- **Default**: `allowBeanDefinitionOverriding` is `null` → treated as `true` → overriding is allowed, no exception.
- **Exception occurs** only when someone explicitly calls `DefaultListableBeanFactory.setAllowBeanDefinitionOverriding(false)` and a second bean/component with the same name is then registered (e.g., two `@Bean` methods with the same name across configs, a duplicate `<bean id="...">`, or a component scan collision).

Since Spring Boot 2.1, `spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding` defaults to `false` in Boot apps (Boot calls `setAllowBeanDefinitionOverriding` under the hood), which is why this exception is commonly seen there even though plain Spring Framework defaults to permissive.

## How applications commonly avoid it

- Ensure bean names are unique (rename one of the conflicting `@Bean` methods/XML ids, or use `@Bean(name = "...")`).
- If overriding is intentional (e.g., a test config or an addon deliberately replacing a bean), either explicitly allow it via `setAllowBeanDefinitionOverriding(true)` / `spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding=true`, or use `BeanDefinitionRegistrar`/`BeanDefinitionCustomizer` patterns designed for override, rather than relying on the blanket flag.
- For fine-grained control (Spring Framework 6.2+), implement `isBeanDefinitionOverridable(String beanName)` (declared on `BeanDefinitionRegistry`, `spring-beans/.../BeanDefinitionRegistry.java:55`) to allow overriding per-name instead of globally.

## Why it can throw

`DefaultListableBeanFactory.registerBeanDefinition` (`spring-beans/.../DefaultListableBeanFactory.java:1268-1271`) checks whether a bean name is already registered:

```java
BeanDefinition existingDefinition = this.beanDefinitionMap.get(beanName);
if (existingDefinition != null) {
    if (!isBeanDefinitionOverridable(beanName)) {
        throw new BeanDefinitionOverrideException(beanName, beanDefinition, existingDefinition);
    }
    ...
```

`isBeanDefinitionOverridable` (line 1447-1449) just delegates to `isAllowBeanDefinitionOverriding()` (line 279-281), which defaults to `true` (`!Boolean.FALSE.equals(this.allowBeanDefinitionOverriding)`). So a second definition for the same bean name is normally *allowed* and just logged (`logBeanDefinitionOverriding`), overwriting the map entry — no exception. The exception only fires when overriding has been explicitly disabled.

A parallel check exists for aliases (line 1281-1289): registering a bean whose name collides with an existing *alias* throws the same exception if overriding isn't allowed, or a `BeanDefinitionStoreException` if the alias points nowhere.

## When it happens in practice

You get `BeanDefinitionOverrideException` when:
1. `DefaultListableBeanFactory.setAllowBeanDefinitionOverriding(false)` has been called explicitly, **and**
2. two bean definitions are registered under the same name (e.g., two `@Bean` methods with the same name, a `@Component` colliding with an XML/`@Bean` definition, or importing a config twice).

Spring Boot sets this to `false` by default since Boot 2.1 (`spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding=false`), which is why this exception is commonly associated with Boot apps, even though in plain Spring Framework the default (`true`) is permissive.

`isBeanDefinitionOverridable(String beanName)` is also `protected`/overridable per-bean-name — subclasses can override it to allow overriding for some names but not others, independent of the global flag.

## How applications commonly avoid it

- Don't disable overriding unless intentional; if it must stay disabled (e.g., Boot's default), give conflicting beans distinct names/qualifiers so they don't collide.
- Explicitly set `@Bean(name = "...")` or component names to avoid accidental collisions from classpath scanning + `@Configuration` overlap.
- If overriding is genuinely desired in a specific spot, either call `setAllowBeanDefinitionOverriding(true)` on the factory (Boot: `spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding=true`), or override `isBeanDefinitionOverridable(beanName)` in a custom registry to whitelist just that name.
- `ConfigurationClassBeanDefinitionReader` (one of the grep hits) catches this exception during `@Configuration` class processing to produce a clearer error message pointing at the conflicting `@Bean` methods, which is usually the actual signal developers see and act on.

In `PostProcessorRegistrationDelegate.invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors` (`spring-context/.../support/PostProcessorRegistrationDelegate.java:68`):

1. **`BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor` (BDRPP) phase** runs first, in three passes — `PriorityOrdered` (lines 107–119), `Ordered` (121–132), then a `while (reiterate)` loop for the rest (134–150). Each pass calls `beanFactory.getBeanNamesForType(BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor.class, ...)` **fresh** before processing, and the final loop keeps re-querying (`reiterate = true` whenever a new, unprocessed BDRPP name shows up) until a full pass finds nothing new. So if a BDRPP registers another BDRPP bean definition, that new one is picked up and invoked in the same `refresh()` call — `processedBeans` (a `HashSet<String>`) is used to avoid re-invoking ones already run.

2. **Plain `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` phase** (lines 162–204) happens afterward: it again calls `getBeanNamesForType(BeanFactoryPostProcessor.class, ...)` against the now-mutated registry, so any new plain BFPP bean definitions added during phase 1 (or by earlier BFPPs in this phase, since names are looked up once at line 164/172 before instantiation — note this list is captured once, unlike the BDRPP loop) are picked up too, sorted by `PriorityOrdered`/`Ordered`/plain and invoked in order, skipping anything in `processedBeans`.

Key asymmetry: BDRPPs get the "reiterate until stable" treatment because they're expected to register more definitions (including more processors); the plain-`BeanFactoryPostProcessor` list is fetched once per priority tier, so a *plain* BFPP that registers a brand-new BFPP bean definition mid-phase-2 won't retroactively get added to an already-built tier list — though it would still be caught by `getBeanNamesForType` at the *next* tier's lookup if not yet processed. In practice, this is why Spring strongly recommends implementing bean-registering post-processors as `BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor`, not `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`.

**Mechanism** (`PostProcessorRegistrationDelegate.invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors`, `spring-context/.../support/PostProcessorRegistrationDelegate.java:68`):

1. **BDRPPs are processed in three re-querying passes** — `PriorityOrdered` (lines 107–119), then `Ordered` (121–132), then a `while (reiterate)` loop over "all others" (134–150). Each pass calls `beanFactory.getBeanNamesForType(BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor.class, ...)` **fresh, after** the previous pass ran (lines 108, 122, 138). Since each BDRPP mutates the shared `BeanDefinitionRegistry` directly via `postProcessBeanDefinitionRegistry(registry)` (line 93), any new bean definitions it registers — including new BDRPP beans — become visible to `getBeanNamesForType` in the next pass. The final `while (reiterate)` loop specifically exists to keep re-scanning until no new, unprocessed BDRPP appears (`processedBeans` tracks what's already run), so a BDRPP that registers *another* BDRPP will have that new one picked up and invoked too.

2. **After all BDRPPs finish**, `postProcessBeanFactory()` is invoked on all of them (line 153), then on the regular `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`s (line 154).

3. **Plain `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` beans** (not BDRPPs) are handled afterward in a single, non-reiterating pass: `getBeanNamesForType(BeanFactoryPostProcessor.class, ...)` is called **once** (line 165), split into `PriorityOrdered`/`Ordered`/plain buckets, and invoked in that order (lines 187–204). There's no re-scan loop here — if a `postProcessBeanFactory` call registers a *new* plain `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` bean definition, it will **not** be invoked in this `refresh()` cycle, since the name list was already captured.

**Bottom line**: registering new bean *definitions* (of any kind, including entities later consumed by `BeanPostProcessor`s or normal beans) is always visible to later phases because they all read from the same live registry. But whether a newly-registered *processor bean* itself gets invoked in the same pass depends on its type — `BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor`s get iteratively re-discovered (the `while (reiterate)` loop), while plain `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`s registered by a processor do not get picked up until the next `refresh()`. This asymmetry is why Spring's own extension mechanisms (e.g. `ConfigurationClassPostProcessor`) always implement `BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor` rather than plain `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` when they need to add further post-processors.

## `BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor` (registers definitions) → picked up dynamically

For processors that implement `BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor` (a sub-interface of `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` that can add new `BeanDefinition`s to the registry), `PostProcessorRegistrationDelegate.invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors` (`spring-context/src/main/java/org/springframework/context/support/PostProcessorRegistrationDelegate.java:68`) re-queries the bean factory for processor names *after each phase*, rather than computing the full set once up front:

- Phase 1 (lines 108–119): calls `beanFactory.getBeanNamesForType(BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor.class, ...)`, filters for `PriorityOrdered`, invokes them.
- Phase 2 (lines 121–132): calls `getBeanNamesForType` **again**, filters for `Ordered`, excluding beans already in `processedBeans`.
- Phase 3 (lines 134–150): a `do/while`-style `reiterate` loop that keeps calling `getBeanNamesForType` and invoking any newly-discovered `BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor` beans (including ones just registered by a prior processor in this same loop) until a full pass finds nothing new.

So if processor A (say, `PriorityOrdered`) registers a new bean definition for a class implementing `BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor`, that new processor's name will show up in the next `getBeanNamesForType` call and get invoked in a later phase (Ordered phase, or the catch-all reiterate loop) — even though it didn't exist when `invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors` started. This is exactly why the loop exists: to converge until no more registry post-processors appear.

## Plain `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` (only modifies existing definitions, not registry-aware) → picked up too, but only in the later single pass

After all registry-processing settles (line 153–154, which calls `postProcessBeanFactory` on everything collected so far), the method does one more `getBeanNamesForType(BeanFactoryPostProcessor.class, ...)` at line 164–165, *after* all registry mutation is done. This list naturally includes any new `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` bean definitions that were registered by the registry post-processors above, since it's queried fresh. These are then split into `PriorityOrdered` / `Ordered` / plain buckets and invoked in that order (lines 187–204) — a single set of three passes, not an iterative reiterate loop.

## The asymmetry

- New `BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor`s registered *during* the registry-processing phase are reliably discovered thanks to the `reiterate` loop — this is guaranteed to converge.
- New plain `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`s are only picked up because the final `getBeanNamesForType` call at line 164 happens to run after registry processing completes — there's no re-querying loop for this second block, so a `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` registered by another plain `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` bean at line 200-204 (the "non-ordered" bucket, last to run) would *not* be picked up in the same `refresh()` call, since there's no further pass after line 204.
